opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Pricing for defense customers is different from commercial pricing, and the biggest mistake I see robotics companies make is pricing the hardware as if it were the whole product.

The military doesn't buy a robot. It buys a capability, and that capability includes training, sustainment, spare parts, software updates, and a supply chain it can count on for years. So we start with the mission. What problem does this solve? What does it replace? What does it cost them to do this today, in dollars and, more importantly, in risk to people? If a system keeps a soldier out of a minefield or off a dangerous route clearance mission, that value is enormous. But you can't just put a number on a life and charge for it. That isn't how procurement works, and it isn't the right way to think about it.

In practice we build up from total cost of ownership. Program offices look hard at lifecycle cost, so we're transparent about unit price, but also about what it costs to keep the system running over ten or fifteen years. Sometimes that pushes us toward lower upfront hardware prices and a sustainment or software-subscription model. That's a newer conversation with the services, but they're increasingly open to it, especially as autonomy becomes more software-defined.

The other reality is attritability. Ukraine changed the conversation. If you expect to lose systems in combat, a quarter-million-dollar exquisite robot doesn't make sense when a much cheaper one can do eighty percent of the job. So there's real pressure to design for cost from day one: commercial components where you can, modularity, and production at scale. Price is a design input, not something you figure out at the end.

Finally, you have to understand the contracting vehicle. Pricing for a prototype through an OTA (other transaction authority) looks very different from pricing for a program of record with cost-accounting requirements. Early on you may price aggressively just to get units into soldiers' hands and get feedback. The goal is to earn the right to scale, because volume is what ultimately brings the price down for everyone.

r001.rationale: The response calls subscription pricing a newer conversation but says services are increasingly open to it. It does not identify military budgeting practices as an obstacle.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So pricing for military customers is honestly one of the harder parts of the business, because you're not really pricing a product, you're pricing a capability over a lifecycle.

The first thing I'd say is that the hardware itself is almost never where the value is. If you think of a robot as a piece of metal with motors and sensors, you'll race to the bottom with everyone else who can bend aluminum. What the customer is actually buying is readiness. Can this thing go downrange, in sand, in rain, in cold, with a nineteen-year-old operating it after a few hours of training, and come back? So we try to price around that: uptime, repairability in the field, how fast we can push a software update when the threat changes, how much training burden we're taking off their plate.

The second thing is you have to understand how they buy. A defense customer isn't swiping a credit card. There's a program office, there's a contracting officer, there are color-of-money rules about what budget can pay for what. Research dollars behave differently from procurement dollars, which behave differently from operations and maintenance dollars. So we structure offers to fit those lanes. Sometimes that means a lower upfront unit price with a sustainment contract behind it. Sometimes it means a per-unit price that includes a block of spares and training because that's what they can actually obligate this year.

Third, we're pretty disciplined about not pricing one-off exotic configurations as if they were volume production. If a customer wants something bespoke, we're honest that it's a non-recurring engineering cost and we separate that out. Blending it into the unit price just hides the real economics and makes the next conversation harder.

And then there's a philosophical piece. I think a lot of companies look at defense and see deep pockets and pad everything. I'd push back on that. These are taxpayer dollars, and the people on the other end of the purchase order are going to trust their lives to the thing. If you gouge, you win once. If you're fair and transparent about your cost structure and margins, you end up with a relationship that lasts across programs, and frankly that's worth more than any single contract.

r001.rationale: The response describes military budget categories and says offers must fit those funding lanes, but it does not identify them as an obstacle to subscription pricing.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with the mission: what does the robot need to do, and what does it cost the customer to do that today? Then you have to look beyond the purchase price to training, maintenance, spare parts, and support. A robot that’s inexpensive to buy but difficult to keep operational isn’t a good value.

For military customers, I’d also focus on whether they can afford to deploy it at a useful scale. If it’s so expensive that they’re reluctant to put it in harm’s way, that undermines part of the reason for having a robot. You want a price that supports a reliable product and lets the customer use it where it’s needed.

r001.rationale: The response discusses affordability, purchase price, and operating costs, but does not identify military budgeting practices as an obstacle to subscription pricing.

sol-6.1.text: I’d start with the mission and work backward. What does the robot need to do, what does it cost to deliver that capability reliably, and what will it cost the customer to operate and maintain it? The purchase price is only part of the picture. Training, maintenance, spare parts, and support all matter. You want a price that lets you support the system over its life and lets the customer field enough robots to make a meaningful difference.

r001.rationale: The response discusses purchase and lifecycle costs for military customers, but does not identify military budgeting practices as an obstacle to subscription pricing.
